This week in the engine

The engine is pinned to this week's Lemonade release, the release candidate's checks are green, and two measurements this week say plainly where two slow things stand.

The release candidate#

  • Lemonade: the pin moved to this week's Lemonade release (#641); the fork sync now ports a release onto the fork's main instead of checking out the tag (#642).
  • 1bit OS: the live image passes 17 of 17 checks on the board with Secure Boot on. The image build now refuses an image whose kernel modules were selected for another kernel (#638), and the weekly run signs the sealed NPU kernel sets between build and package (#648).
  • Hardware gate: fully green at the shipping pin, after the HRX bump to llama.cpp d8d2f5b39f22 and hrx-system 82804197bcbe (#659).

The tag and the packages are the owner's; the checklist is on Releases.

Two measurements, stated as they are#

Flash-Next prefill. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next prefills at 287 tok/s on HRX. A prefill forward takes about 1.8 s, of which about 1.0 s is host time between dispatches, not device time. Measured on the file itself, that gap is a GET_ROWS the HRX backend declines, so the operation runs on the host and the device waits (#572, written up in #646 and on HRX). The fix is a kernel, not a setting.

Two engines on the NPU. --npu-streams 2 runs a second resident engine on the NPU (#640). With both engines on whole-array kernels, the aggregate throughput is 0.41x of one engine: they contend for the same array, and each waits for the other. Two engines need kernel sets partitioned to disjoint halves of the array, one column partition per engine, which is #656. Until then the second engine is opt-in and costs more than it gives.

Later the same day#

  • The HRX pin moved again, to a fork head that carries six commits: the host-gap profiler, the KV cache zero-padding repair, the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash port, and the GET_ROWS fix that lets Flash-Next's 320-million-row token table gather on the GPU instead of the CPU (#672, fork #156, #159). Every pin move passes the hardware gate on the board first; the recipe for a hand-raised bump is now written down (#675).
  • ONNX Runtime runs inside the engine, behind a build flag, with our own execution provider. Its first proof is a MatMul on the NPU through an ORT session, repeatable, within 0.5 % of the CPU provider's result; a Quark-quantised A8W8 graph runs on it unchanged. The first whole model through it is not right yet, and the write-up says so (#647, ONNX Runtime).
  • The NPU and the GPU run at the same time. A reported hazard said they could not; forty measured reps say they can, at a cost of about 13 % of the NPU's weight stream while the GPU is busy. The numbers are in Hybrid.
  • The README is simple again: boot a stick, try it, install it; the technical map moved to How the engine is built (#676).
  • The engine became a workload for AMD's Hyperloom tuner (#660), the daily census and bump workflows now report their failures instead of failing silently (#664, #665), and the kernel arena that scores NPU kernels against a byte-exact oracle has its public half in the tree (#668).
